lines: Watch what didn't change here. Not the workload, not the hardware it would've run on — just where it's running.
And the bill went up anyway. Whatever the cloud promised, it isn't delivering it for a workload shaped like this one.
Before the rest of this topic, think about what the cloud's whole pricing story actually depends on.
It depends on a workload having quiet moments to shrink into. This one doesn't have any. What does that do to the math?
answer: No idle time means no discount — the workload pays the full rate around the clock.
Elasticity isn't a universal discount. It's a reward for having somewhere to scale down to, and this workload never does.

lines: Watch what each half of this picture was actually built for, not just what replaced what.
The old estate assumed one specific cluster shape. The new one swaps every piece of that for something general-purpose — storage, scheduling, the engine, the table format, each its own layer now.
Pay attention here, because this is the one thing in the whole topic that's actually running, not just described.
Watch the second write land. That's not a diagram of a snapshot — it's a real one, sitting on a real object store, that you could query back out right now.
Watch what actually happened in this timeline, not just that prices changed.
The licensing model flipped from something you own to something you keep paying for. That's the part that reached almost everyone, and that's the part that made people look elsewhere.
Notice these are four separate tests, not four flavors of the same argument.
Each one either applies to a workload or it doesn't. Say 'on-prem is cheaper' without naming which of these four actually fits, and you haven't really made an argument yet.
Watch what's missing from this picture that was always there before, quietly, in the background.
Nobody refreshes the hardware for you. Nobody runs the cluster for you. And nothing catches you if you guessed capacity wrong.
If you keep one thing: winning one of those four tests and avoiding the operational bill are two completely different claims.

The modern stack replaces the old one piece by piece. A licensing shift, not new technology, triggered the second look. Four tests decide the winner. And the bill doesn't disappear just because on-prem passed one.
Before I answer, look at the shape of this workload again — minutes of real work, then nothing, every single day.
That shape is the opposite of the hook's workload. Does moving it on-prem actually make sense here?
answer: No — this is exactly the shape the cloud's pricing model is built to reward.
Idle time isn't a problem to solve by moving on-prem. It's the one thing elasticity already handles for free.
